feedback: If the frame has the wrong number of straws or connectors, re-establish the target first (12 edges, 8 vertices) and rebuild, counting each piece as it is added.

If the faces are not square, check that all straws are equal length and that the corners are right angles; unequal straws give a cuboid or an irregular frame rather than a cube, and even equal straws can lean into diamond-shaped faces unless the frame is squared up.
Compare the built frame side by side with a real cube-shaped solid to spot missing or extra edges.
activities.intendedInsight: A cube is defined by its structure — 12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces — and building it requires coordinating that structure rather than approximating a box shape.
learnerActions: Before building, predict and count how many edges (straws) and vertices (connectors) a cube needs, and state the target: 12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces.
Build the cube frame, snapping straws (edges) onto connectors (balls of clay or plastic joints for vertices).

Check that every straw is the same length and that the corners are square (right angles, not leaning), because equal straws alone can still give a squashed frame with diamond-shaped faces; then compare the finished frame against a real cube-shaped solid.
Point to and count the edges, vertices and faces on the completed frame to confirm the structure.
Try building a cuboid with edges of different lengths as a contrast and describe how it differs from the cube (not all edges equal, so some faces are rectangles that are not squares).
activities.title: Build a cube frame from straws and connectors

feedback: If the child renames a point-down or sideways shape, hand them the same object and let them rotate it continuously so they see it never changed into something else.
Redirect naming to invariant properties (triangular faces meeting at an apex) rather than to a remembered picture of its usual position.
The point-down pyramid is often a hard case — linger there and ask the child to name the faces they can see and feel.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name comes from properties that do not change when it is rotated or viewed from a new angle; turning a solid does not make it a different shape.
learnerActions: Hold a real pyramid (or cube) and physically turn it: point-up, on its side, point-down, and viewed from directly above.
At each orientation, say what the shape is and how you know, naming it by its properties (e.g. 'a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex').
State explicitly whether the name changed when the shape turned, and explain why it should not.
Repeat with a cuboid laid on different faces, confirming it is the same solid each time.
activities.title: Rotate a solid and keep naming it

feedback: If the figure is not closed, return to the starting dot and count sides until the path closes.
If a side is curved, redraw it as a straight segment between two dots.
If there are too few or too many sides, re-count aloud while re-drawing, marking each side as it is placed.
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate 2-D shape is a closed figure with the correct number of straight sides; its name depends on properties such as closure, side count and, for shapes like rectangles, right angles, not on size.
learnerActions: Draw named 2-D shapes (triangle, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon) on dotted paper or a geoboard.
Count and mark each side as it is drawn, keeping track so the figure closes with the right number of straight sides.
After drawing, re-count the sides and check the shape is closed and has straight (not curved) edges.
Draw the same shape again at a different size and confirm it keeps its name (a bigger hexagon is still a hexagon).
activities.title: Draw 2-D shapes accurately on dotted paper or a geoboard

feedback: If the child cannot see a face as a 2-D shape, lay the net flat and trace one face, then fold it back into place on the solid.
Count the faces on both net and solid to confirm they match.
Note that a folded card net is a thin physical approximation of the ideal solid, which has zero-thickness faces — it stands in for the mathematical shape it represents.
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a solid is a 2-D shape, so 2-D and 3-D shape knowledge connect: a cube's faces are squares, a pyramid's faces include triangles.
learnerActions: Fold a net into a solid, then identify each face as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
For a built cube frame, point out where each square face sits between four edges.
Match the faces on the net to the faces on the solid, naming the 2-D shape of each (square, triangle).
activities.title: Link nets and faces to the built solid
